concepts.title: Sums of Consecutive Numbers
concepts.definition: A run of whole numbers that grows by one at each step is a consecutive run, and many totals can be rebuilt out of such runs; one total may even come from several runs of different lengths, for instance 15 works as 7+8, as 4+5+6 and as 1+2+3+4+5.
concepts.formula: total_sum = 4 * first_num + 6 (run of four consecutive terms)
concepts.key_idea: Four consecutive terms carry 0+1+2+3 = 6 beyond four times the first term, so the first term is (total - 6) / 4.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp105.txt lines 1-32 (Anshu's consecutive sums), 696 (Figure it Out Q1)

solution_steps.action: add the fixed offsets of the four terms
solution_steps.explain: The terms n, n+1, n+2, n+3 carry 0+1+2+3 = 6 beyond 4n.

solution_steps.action: remove the offset and divide by 4
solution_steps.explain: Whatever remains after taking away the offset is 4 times the first term.

concepts.title: Same Parity of a +/- b +/- c +/- d Combinations
concepts.definition: Join four letter-numbers with any mix of plus and minus signs and every one of the eight possible expressions lands on the same parity: swapping any single sign shifts the value by twice that letter-number, an even shift, so an even total stays even and an odd total stays odd.
concepts.formula: value_shift = 2 * letter_num (even, for any single sign flip)
concepts.key_idea: Each sign flip moves the total by an even amount, so all eight expressions are parity twins.
question_patterns: place plus and minus signs between 3 4 5 6 in all eight ways and compare the results

solution_steps.action: flip one sign and measure the change
solution_steps.explain: (a + b - c - d) - (a - b - c - d) = 2b, which is even, so the two values agree in parity.

solution_steps.action: apply the parity rules for sums and differences
solution_steps.explain: odd +/- odd = even, even +/- even = even, odd +/- even = odd; hence a +/- b keeps a fixed parity.
Any two of the eight expressions differ by a chain of even shifts, so every placement shares one parity.

concepts.title: Spotting Expressions That Are Always Even
concepts.definition: An algebraic expression is guaranteed even exactly when a factor 2 comes out of it cleanly: 4m and 2q each carry a factor 2, so 4m + 2q equals 2(2m + q) and stays even for every integer choice of m and q, while x^2 + 2 switches parity with x and is only sometimes even.
concepts.key_idea: Factor 2 out of the whole expression; a clean factorisation proves the expression never turns odd.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp105.txt lines 165-254 (Breaking Even, 4m + 2q discussion, x^2 + 2 example)

solution_steps.explain: 4m is a multiple of 4, hence always even.
2q is even as well, and even plus even remains even.

concepts.title: Remainder Classes of Numbers
concepts.definition: Dividing by a fixed divisor sorts whole numbers into remainder classes: the numbers leaving remainder 3 on division by 5 are exactly those 3 above a multiple of 5, written 5k + 3, and the very same class can be dressed as 5k - 2 with k at least 1, since one class can sit r above one multiple or n - r below the next.
concepts.key_idea: Remainder r modulo n means n times k plus r; describing the class as n*k - (n - r) gives a second valid form.

solution_steps.explain: Members of the class sit on multiples of the divisor, divisor times k.
Adding r lifts the multiple into the chosen remainder class.

concepts.title: Digit-Sum Test for Divisibility by 9
concepts.definition: Every place value sits exactly one above a multiple of 9, since 1, 10, 100, 1000 are 0+1, 9+1, 99+1, 999+1; a whole number therefore exceeds some multiple of 9 by the total of its digits, so it divides evenly by 9 precisely when that digit total does, and the digit total's residue is the number's remainder.
concepts.key_idea: Powers of 10 run one ahead of multiples of 9, so the digits alone carry the whole remainder.
question_patterns: check without dividing whether 93547 is divisible by 9

solution_steps.explain: Each place value is one above a multiple of 9, so the digits carry the entire excess.
The residue of the digit total mod 9 is the residue of the number itself.

concepts.title: Alternating-Sum Test for Divisibility by 11
concepts.definition: Place values alternate between one above and one below multiples of 11, since 1, 10, 100, 1000 give remainders 1, -1, 1, -1; so adding the digits of alternate places and subtracting the rest measures the excess or shortfall, and a number divides by 11 exactly when this alternating total is 0 or a multiple of 11.
concepts.key_idea: The alternating digit total tells how far the number sits from its nearest multiple of 11.

solution_steps.action: alternate plus and minus signs from the units place
solution_steps.explain: Digits in 1, 100, 10000 places are added; digits in 10, 1000, 100000 places are subtracted.
A zero or multiple-of-11 result means divisibility; any other residue is the remainder.

concepts.title: Digital Root by Repeated Digit Addition
concepts.definition: Adding a number's digits, then repeating on the outcome until a single digit survives, produces the digital root; this fingerprint equals the remainder on division by 9, with root 9 standing for remainder 0, a checking method recorded in Aryabhata II's Mahasiddhanta around 950 CE.
concepts.formula: dig_root = number_val % 9 (a residue of 0 is reported as 9)
concepts.key_idea: The digital root is the mod-9 fingerprint of a number; multiples of 9 always root to 9.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp105.txt lines 1235-1281 (digital roots, 489710 example, history note)

solution_steps.explain: 9a and 36b are multiples of 9, so only the leftover 13 = 9 + 4 shapes the root.
The residue mod 9 is the digital root; a residue of 0 is reported as root 9.

concepts.title: Divisibility Laws for Always-Sometimes-Never Claims
concepts.definition: Four structural laws settle most divisibility claims: numbers divisible by one divisor stay divisible after adding or subtracting, every multiple of a multiple inherits the divisibility, divisibility by a number forces divisibility by each of its factors, and divisibility by two numbers forces divisibility by their LCM; matching a claim to these laws sorts it into always, sometimes or never true.
concepts.formula: k divides m_num and k divides n_num implies k divides m_num + n_num
concepts.key_idea: Classify each claim against a divisibility law, then seal the verdict with an example and a counterexample.

solution_steps.action: match the claim to a divisibility law
solution_steps.explain: Sum-difference, multiple-of-multiple, factor and LCM laws each decide one family of claims.

solution_steps.action: back true cases with the algebraic form
solution_steps.explain: Writing the numbers as k*p and k*q turns their total into k*(p + q), still divisible by k.

solution_steps.action: refute over-strong claims with a counterexample
solution_steps.explain: 12 divides by 4 and by 6 yet not by 24, because 4 and 6 share the extra factor 2.

concepts.title: Cryptarithms - Letters Standing for Digits
concepts.definition: A cryptarithm hides one fixed digit behind each letter, gives different letters different digits, and never allows a leading zero; solving runs column by column from the units place, letting carries and product sizes pin letters down, as when PQ x 8 = RS forces the two-digit factor to stay at most 12.
concepts.key_idea: Climb the columns: units first, carry forward, and bound each letter by the size of the answer.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp105.txt lines 1282-1348 (Digits in Disguise, PQ x 8 and BYE x 6), 1850-1884 (answers)

solution_steps.explain: The size of the answer limits its hundreds letter, and a two-digit product limits both factors.
The units digit of the sum or product restricts the unit letters modulo 10.
Each carry narrows the choices; the solve ends with every column consistent and no digit repeated.
